label: RCA Victor
description: Waylon Jennings was still easing out of Chet Atkins-produced Nashville polish when he cut this transitional record, taking its title track from Lee Clayton and pushing toward a tougher, road-band sound. Jessi Colter joins him on a cover of "Under Your Spell Again," a preview of the real-life partnership that would anchor the outlaw scene. It is rougher and less unified than the albums that followed, but the title song gave the whole movement one of its slogans.
lineage: Grows out of Jennings's early-1970s push against RCA's countrypolitan production, and points directly at the fuller outlaw sound he found the next year on Honky Tonk Heroes.

label: RCA Victor
description: Recorded soon after Jennings won a measure of creative control from RCA, this is the sound of a Nashville insider assembling his own studio band instead of using staff pickers. The Steve Young title track and covers of Kris Kristofferson and Willie Nelson songs establish the songwriter-first ethic that defined outlaw country, sung in Jennings's unhurried baritone drawl. It set the template of a stable touring band and hand-picked songs that Honky Tonk Heroes would perfect a few months later.
lineage: Follows directly from Jennings's contract renegotiation with RCA and feeds straight into Honky Tonk Heroes; its title track comes from fellow outlaw precursor Steve Young.
key_tracks: Good Time Charlie's Got the Blues

label: RCA Victor
description: Waylon Jennings built this record almost entirely from songs by a then-unknown Billy Joe Shaver, after meeting him at the 1972 Dripping Springs Reunion in Texas. The road-worn character sketches, Ralph Mooney's crying steel guitar, and Jennings's own touring band standing in for Nashville session players make this the outlaw movement's founding document. It is tighter and more unified than anything Jennings had made before, and its mix of songwriter's voice and bar-band grit set the terms for the rest of the decade.
lineage: Draws directly on Billy Joe Shaver's songwriting and points forward to every Jennings, David Allan Coe and Johnny Paycheck record that followed; the hinge point between Nashville countrypolitan and outlaw country.
key_tracks: Old Five and Dimers Like Me

label: RCA Victor
description: The first album Jennings produced entirely on his own, cut at his own pace with his touring band rather than Nashville's staff producers. The title track became a hit ballad, but the record's loose, unhurried feel matters more than any single song, closer to a bar band warming up than a polished single factory. It shows the outlaw arrangement of artist-as-producer and songs chosen on his own terms already working as a commercial strategy.
lineage: Extends the self-produced model Jennings won the right to use after Lonesome, On'ry and Mean and Honky Tonk Heroes, cementing his independence within RCA's Nashville system.
key_tracks: It's Not Supposed to Be That Way

label: RCA Victor
description: Often singled out as Jennings's most personal record, built around slower, reflective songs like "Dreaming My Dreams with You" and "Waymore's Blues." Producer Jack Clement leaves space around the rhythm section, letting Jennings's baritone carry songs about loneliness and the cost of the road rather than outlaw swagger. It remains a favorite in his own catalog for its unguarded, road-worn tone.
lineage: Comes between the outlaw movement's commercial breakthrough on Are You Ready for the Country and its peak on Ol' Waylon, showing the quieter side of the same songwriter-first approach.
key_tracks: Are You Sure Hank Done It This Way

album: Are You Ready for the Country
label: RCA Victor
description: Jennings covers Neil Young's title track and leans harder into rock instrumentation than before, while originals like "Old Friend" keep the record grounded in his own voice. Released the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, it rode the movement's crossover into rock and pop audiences without losing its Telecaster-and-steel core. The record shows how porous the line had become between outlaw country and the Crazy Horse-style rock it increasingly resembled.
lineage: Its title-track cover of Neil Young links the outlaw scene directly to the Crazy Horse lineage the wider atlas traces, arriving right at the commercial peak Wanted! The Outlaws would soon confirm.
key_tracks: Are You Ready for the Country

label: RCA Victor
description: Jennings's commercial high point, built around "Luckenbach, Texas" and covers ranging from Kenny Rogers's "Lucille" to Neil Diamond's "Sweet Caroline." The record shows outlaw country at its most confident and pop-friendly, still driven by the same road band but polished enough to top both country and pop charts. It cemented Jennings as the movement's biggest commercial draw alongside Willie Nelson.
lineage: Represents outlaw country's full absorption into the mainstream that Wanted! The Outlaws had opened up the year before.
key_tracks: Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love)
I Think I'm Gonna Kill Myself

label: RCA Victor
description: The first full studio pairing of Jennings and Nelson as billed equals, anchored by the Ed and Patsy Bruce song "Mammas Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys," which became the outlaw movement's biggest crossover hit. Kristofferson and Lee Clayton songs sit alongside a surprising Fleetwood Mac cover, all filtered through the two singers' interlocking drawls. It is the commercial peak of the Waylon-Willie partnership that Wanted! The Outlaws had introduced two years earlier.
lineage: Follows Wanted! The Outlaws in pairing Jennings and Nelson as a duo act, and its hit single made the outlaw brand a household name beyond country radio.
key_tracks: Mammas Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys
I Can Get Off on You
The Wurlitzer Prize (I Don't Want to Get Over You)

label: RCA Victor
description: Jennings answers his own outlaw mythology directly on "Don't You Think This Outlaw Bit's Done Got Out of Hand," recorded not long after a well-publicized 1977 drug arrest. A Buddy Holly medley and covers of Johnny Cash and Merle Haggard root the record in his Texas rock and roll roots as much as outlaw swagger. It is one of the few outlaw records to openly question the outlaw image while still trading on it.
lineage: A self-aware sequel to Ol' Waylon and Wanted! The Outlaws, turning the movement's own marketing into songwriting material.
key_tracks: Don't You Think This Outlaw Bit's Done Got Out of Hand

label: RCA Victor
description: A loose concept album Willie Nelson wrote and largely shaped himself while still under RCA contract, tracing what he called "the Imperfect Man" from birth to death through spoken interludes and short songs. RCA gave it little push, but it previewed the narrative song-cycle approach Nelson used much more famously on Red Headed Stranger four years later. Sparse piano and his own unhurried phrasing carry the record more than any single hit.
lineage: The first sign of the stripped-down, self-directed concept-album approach Nelson perfected on Red Headed Stranger, made while he was still pushing RCA for creative control.

label: Atlantic Records
description: Willie Nelson's first album after moving back to Austin and signing with Atlantic, cut with a looser, funkier band than Nashville had ever let him use. "Whiskey River" opens the record and became his lifelong concert opener, while the ragged title track and horn-flecked arrangements mix Bakersfield twang with soul and jazz phrasing. It is generally treated as the moment Nelson found his own sound after years of writing hits for other singers.
lineage: Marks Nelson's break from Nashville production and the start of the Austin-based, genre-blending style that runs through Phases and Stages and Red Headed Stranger.

label: Atlantic Records
description: A concept album about a marriage's collapse, side one narrated from the wife's point of view and side two from the husband's, recorded at Muscle Shoals with a soul rhythm section. "Bloody Mary Morning" and "Pretend I Never Happened" turn plainspoken divorce into some of Nelson's sharpest songwriting. The record's dual-perspective structure was a direct dry run for the story album he made next, Red Headed Stranger.
lineage: Builds on Shotgun Willie's Atlantic-era freedom and rehearses the story-album format Nelson used on Red Headed Stranger the following year.
key_tracks: (How Will I Know) I'm Falling in Love Again

label: Columbia Records
description: Willie Nelson's first album for Columbia under a contract giving him full creative control, used to record a stark concept album about a preacher who murders his unfaithful wife, arranged with almost nothing but his own guitar, sister Bobbie's piano, and occasional harmonica. Columbia executives reportedly thought it sounded like a demo tape; it became a number-one country album and Nelson's commercial breakthrough. Its bare-bones production, built around the old parlor song "Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain," is now treated as one of the most consequential sonic choices in 1970s country.
lineage: The culmination of the narrative concept-album approach Nelson tried on Yesterday's Wine and Phases and Stages, proving outlaw country's stripped-down aesthetic could top the charts.
key_tracks: Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain

label: Columbia Records
description: A gospel album recorded in 1973 for Atlantic, shelved when the label balked at releasing it, and finally issued by Columbia after Red Headed Stranger's success gave Nelson leverage. He runs well-worn hymns like "Uncloudy Day" and "Will the Circle Be Unbroken" through the same honky-tonk band feel as his secular records, treating gospel and outlaw country as branches of the same plainspoken tradition. It reached number one on the country album chart despite being pure church music.
lineage: A sibling record to Shotgun Willie and Phases and Stages from the same Atlantic sessions period, delayed until Nelson's Columbia-era commercial power got it released.

label: Columbia Records
description: Nelson's second Columbia album folds a warm reading of "That Lucky Old Sun" and a long medley of his own earlier hits ("Funny How Time Slips Away," "Crazy," "Night Life") into a relaxed, jazz-inflected country sound. It topped the country album chart the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, showing Nelson could sustain commercial momentum without repeating Red Headed Stranger's stark formula. The record leans toward the warm, standards-minded direction he pushed further on Stardust two years later.
lineage: Sits between Red Headed Stranger's austerity and Stardust's full embrace of pop standards, both records grown out of the creative control Nelson won at Columbia.
key_tracks: If You've Got the Money (I've Got the Time)
That Lucky Old Sun (Just Rolls Around Heaven All Day)

label: Columbia Records
description: A full album of tribute to honky-tonk singer Lefty Frizzell, recut in Nelson's own loping phrasing rather than straight imitation. It doubles as a reminder that the outlaw generation saw itself as heirs to hard country rather than rebels against it: Frizzell's behind-the-beat vocal style shaped Nelson's own singing as much as anything in Nashville. It is a quieter, more traditionalist record than Red Headed Stranger, made to honor a hero rather than to make a statement.
lineage: Connects the outlaw movement directly back to honky-tonk forebear Lefty Frizzell, the hard-country tradition this lane's style vocabulary is drawn from.

label: Columbia Records
description: Nelson set country songwriting aside almost entirely to record ten American pop standards, "Georgia on My Mind," "Blue Skies," "All of Me," with producer Booker T. Jones and a spare, jazz-leaning combo. It was a commercial gamble Columbia resisted, then a multi-platinum hit that stayed on the country charts for years and widened what an outlaw-era country record could sound like. The relaxed, behind-the-beat phrasing that made him a country singer works just as well on Hoagy Carmichael as on Merle Haggard.
lineage: Extends the pop-standards move hinted at on The Sound in Your Mind's medley into a full album, using the creative freedom Nelson's outlaw-era Columbia deal secured him.

album: Old Five and Dimers Like Me
label: Monument Records
description: Billy Joe Shaver's debut as a singer, recording his own versions of the same working-class character songs Waylon Jennings had just built Honky Tonk Heroes around. His voice is rougher and less polished than Jennings's, closer to plainspoken talking-blues than pop country, which suits songs about drifting, prison and hard luck. It never sold like Jennings's version but stands as the definitive reading of songs that became outlaw-country standards.
lineage: The songwriter's-own-voice companion to Honky Tonk Heroes, and a direct influence on the plainspoken storytelling later carried forward by Steve Earle and Todd Snider.
key_tracks: Old Five and Dimers Like Me
Willy the Wandering Gypsy and Me
I Been to Georgia on a Fast Train

label: Capricorn Records
description: Shaver's second album moved him from Monument to Capricorn, the Southern-rock label behind the Allman Brothers, giving these songs a slightly heavier backing band than his debut. "Ride Me Down Easy" and the title track keep his talking-blues phrasing and plainspoken Texas detail intact even as the arrangements get rowdier. It is a transitional record between the bare honky-tonk of his debut and the fuller rock band he used on Gypsy Boy.
lineage: Follows Old Five and Dimers Like Me and, through the Capricorn Records connection, links Shaver's outlaw songwriting to the Southern-rock scene around the Allman Brothers.

label: Capricorn Records
description: Shaver's third album, still on Capricorn, revisits "Honky Tonk Heroes" in his own arrangement and adds new road songs like "Chicken on the Ground" and the title track. It carries the same unpolished, first-person storytelling as his other 1970s records, closer to a folksinger backed by a bar band than a Nashville production. Commercially it did little, but it deepened the songbook other outlaw artists kept drawing from.
lineage: Closes out Shaver's Capricorn run alongside When I Get My Wings, continuing the plainspoken songwriting that shaped Waylon Jennings's outlaw sound.

label: Monument Records
description: Kris Kristofferson's debut set the songwriter-first template the outlaw movement built on, introducing "Me and Bobby McGee," "Sunday Mornin' Comin' Down" and "Help Me Make It Through the Night," songs that became hits for Janis Joplin, Johnny Cash and Sammi Smith before Kristofferson's own limited, conversational voice found its audience. Producer Fred Foster kept the arrangements simple, letting the literary, plainspoken lyrics carry the songs. It arrived a year before the outlaw movement's usual starting point but supplied much of its songwriting backbone.
lineage: Predates Waylon Jennings's and Willie Nelson's outlaw breakthroughs by several years but supplied key songs and the literary-songwriter model both men built on.
key_tracks: Help Me Make It Through the Night
borderline_note: Released in 1970, just before V23's 1971 start date, but its songs and songwriter-first model directly shaped the outlaw movement that followed.

album: The Silver Tongued Devil and I
label: Monument Records
description: Kristofferson's second album is more assured than his debut, built around the confessional title track and "The Pilgrim, Chapter 33," a composite portrait of the drifting singer-songwriters around him. His limited, talk-singing voice matters less than the density of the writing, which set a bar the rest of the outlaw scene's songwriters measured themselves against. It remains the record most critics point to as his best.
lineage: Cements the confessional-songwriter model Kristofferson introduced on his debut, an influence Waylon Jennings and Billy Joe Shaver both drew on directly.
key_tracks: The Silver Tongued Devil and I

label: Monument Records
description: Named for its John Prine-referencing title track, this record mixes gospel-inflected songwriting with barbed class commentary on "Enough for You" and "Nobody Wins." It is looser and more political than Kristofferson's first two albums, reflecting his growing engagement with counterculture and anti-establishment themes inside a Nashville format. Fred Foster and Dennis Linde's production keeps it warm rather than preachy.
lineage: Extends the socially conscious songwriting strand Kristofferson opened on his first two Monument albums, a thread that fellow Nashville outsiders like Bobby Bare and Tompall Glaser would echo.
key_tracks: Jesus Was a Capricorn (Owed to John Prine)

label: Monument Records
description: A darker, more self-lacerating record than Kristofferson's earlier albums, recorded in Los Angeles as his marriage to Rita Coolidge and his own drinking were both under strain. Songs like "Star-Spangled Bummer" and "Rescue Mission" trade the earlier records' romantic confidence for exhaustion and self-doubt. It is less celebrated than his early-1970s run but is a key document of the toll outlaw-scene excess took on its own songwriters.
lineage: A bleaker sequel to Jesus Was a Capricorn, reflecting the same Nashville-outsider songwriting tradition turned inward.

album: Tompall (Sings the Songs of Shel Silverstein)
label: MGM Records
description: Tompall Glaser, whose Nashville studio Hillbilly Central became the outlaw movement's clubhouse, devoted this album entirely to songs by Shel Silverstein, whose funny-sad, plainspoken writing suited Glaser's gruff, unhurried baritone. It sits between novelty and heartbreak the way Silverstein's own catalog does, closer to storytelling folk than polished Nashville product. The record is a reminder that the scene's key institution was as much a songwriting salon as a recording studio.
lineage: Made at Glaser's own Hillbilly Central studio, the physical hub where Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson and other outlaw artists worked outside RCA's Nashville system.
key_tracks: Put Another Log on the Fire
Country Gospel Good Book Rock & Roll

album: The Great Tompall and His Outlaw Band
label: MGM Records
description: Recorded at Hillbilly Central right as Wanted! The Outlaws made outlaw a marketing category, this album leans into the label with a cover of Hank Thompson's classic Wild Side of Life and a version of Good Hearted Woman, the song Glaser co-wrote with Waylon Jennings. Glaser's road band gives the record a "live in the room" feel closer to a bar gig than a Nashville session. It plays almost like an official statement of purpose from the outlaw movement's key organizer.
lineage: Made in the same Hillbilly Central studio and the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, by one of that compilation's four featured artists.

label: Capitol Records
description: Jessi Colter's Capitol debut, written and largely self-produced, turned the wistful title song "I'm Not Lisa" into a number-one country hit and a rare woman-led entry in a scene dominated by men. Her hushed alto and spare piano-based arrangements sit closer to Laurel Canyon singer-songwriter records than to the road-band sound on her husband Waylon Jennings's albums. It made her the outlaw movement's most visible female voice.
lineage: Recorded at the height of the Nashville outlaw scene her husband Waylon Jennings and Tompall Glaser were building, but in a quieter, more introspective register than either man's records.

label: Capitol Records
description: Colter's second Capitol album of 1976 balances her own compositions with countrified readings of the Beatles' Get Back and Hey Jude, unusual choices for a Nashville-adjacent outlaw record. The title track, written by Muscle Shoals songwriters Donnie Fritts and Spooner Oldham, and the wry "You Hung the Moon (Didn't You Waylon)" keep the record anchored in her marriage to Waylon Jennings and the scene around them. It shows Colter stretching beyond the singer-songwriter mode of her debut.
lineage: A quick Capitol follow-up to I'm Jessi Colter, released the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, on which Colter also appeared.
key_tracks: You Hung the Moon (Didn't You Waylon)

label: Capitol Records
description: A more overtly spiritual record than Colter's first two albums, featuring the trio performance "I Belong to Him" with Waylon Jennings and Roy Orbison. Gospel-leaning songs about faith and devotion reflect Colter's own beliefs more directly than the outlaw scene's usual drinking-and-heartbreak subject matter. It is a quieter, more devotional turn from an artist otherwise associated with the Nashville outlaw crowd.
lineage: Continues Colter's Capitol run alongside I'm Jessi Colter and Diamond in the Rough, while its guest spot from Roy Orbison ties the outlaw scene back to an earlier generation of Nashville-adjacent singers.

label: SSS International Records
description: David Allan Coe's debut, cut soon after his release from prison, is closer to raw electric blues than Nashville country, full of first-person songs about incarceration, addiction and death sung in a rough, unpolished growl. It predates the outlaw movement's commercial rise by several years but set the confrontational, autobiographical persona Coe carried into his mid-1970s Columbia records. Little of it charted, but it remains the rawest document of Coe's own hard-luck mythology.
lineage: Establishes the ex-convict persona and blues-rooted grit that Coe carried into The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy and his later Columbia albums.
borderline_note: More electric blues than country and released in 1970, before the outlaw movement's usual start date, but it originates the ex-convict persona that defines David Allan Coe's outlaw-era records.

label: Columbia Records
description: Coe's major-label debut for Columbia introduced the rhinestone-suited, half-mythical persona he wore for the rest of the decade, mixing his own songs with an early cover of Guy Clark's "Desperados Waiting for a Train." It is more melodic and country than the raw blues of Penitentiary Blues, while keeping the outsider, jailbird backstory front and center in songs like Crazy Mary. The record established Coe as a Nashville curiosity, too strange for mainstream country radio but embraced by the outlaw audience.
lineage: Coe's first Columbia record after Penitentiary Blues, and the start of a run of albums (Once Upon a Rhyme, Longhaired Redneck) that made him one of outlaw country's most theatrical figures.

label: Columbia Records
description: Coe's second Columbia album is best known for its closing track, Steve Goodman and John Prine's "You Never Even Called Me by My Name," a self-aware joke about what makes "the perfect country and western song" that became one of Coe's signature numbers. The rest of the record sticks to the plainspoken road-and-heartbreak songwriting of his debut, still built around Telecaster and pedal steel. It shows Coe as a song interpreter as much as a writer, willing to lean on outside material when it served his persona.
lineage: A direct sequel to The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy, and its closing track ties Coe to the Prine and Goodman school of funny-sad songwriting that runs through the wider atlas.
key_tracks: You Never Even Called Me by My Name
Would You Lay with Me (In a Field of Stone)

label: Columbia Records
description: The first Coe album made up entirely of his own or co-written material, and his most direct statement of outlaw identity, with the title track answering critics who doubted his outsider credibility. It leans harder into the biker-and-outlaw self-image that defined Coe's mid-1970s persona than his more song-interpreter-focused earlier records. AllMusic has singled it out as essential outlaw country, and its rowdier, more self-mythologizing tone set the template for the rest of Coe's Columbia run.
lineage: Coe's declaration of independence within the outlaw scene, building directly on the persona introduced on The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy.

label: Columbia Records
description: Opens with "Willie, Waylon and Me," Coe's own tongue-in-cheek claim to outlaw royalty, and keeps a loose, comic tone throughout with songs like The Punkin Center Barn Dance. It is one of Coe's more good-humored records, trading some of Longhaired Redneck's chip-on-the-shoulder defiance for storytelling closer to novelty. The title nods to his outlaw-movie self-image, a persona he leaned into harder than almost anyone else in the scene.
lineage: Continues the outlaw self-mythology Coe built across his Columbia albums, explicitly naming Jennings and Nelson as his peers on the opening track.

label: Columbia Records
description: A song-heavy, relatively subdued record compared to Longhaired Redneck's outlaw posturing, built around ballads like "Play Me a Sad Song" and a cover of Mickey Newbury's "San Francisco Mabel Joy." Coe leans on outside songwriters (Jay Bolotin, Bobby Charles) as much as his own pen, giving the record a more varied, less one-note feel than some of his other mid-1970s albums. It is a lesser-known entry in his Columbia run but shows a more melodic, less confrontational side of his persona.
lineage: Released the same year as Rides Again, continuing Coe's prolific mid-decade run on Columbia.
key_tracks: Just to Prove My Love for You

label: Epic Records
description: Produced by Billy Sherrill, this album's title track, referencing the maximum county-jail sentence, previewed the working-class, brushes-with-the-law persona Paycheck rode to his biggest hit the following year. His voice is grittier and less polished than the countrypolitan singers Sherrill usually produced, closer to the hard-country tradition of George Jones than to string-laden Nashville pop. It set up Paycheck's run of outlaw-adjacent hits in the late 1970s.
lineage: The Billy Sherrill-produced Epic Records run that connects Paycheck to hard-country forebear George Jones, and a direct lead-in to Take This Job and Shove It the following year.
key_tracks: That's What the Outlaws in Texas Want to Hear

album: Take This Job and Shove It
label: Epic Records
description: Built around a title track written by David Allan Coe about quitting a hated job, this became Paycheck's only number-one hit and the closest thing outlaw country had to a blue-collar protest anthem. The rest of the album sticks to the same barroom, working-man subject matter in Billy Sherrill's tighter, more radio-ready production. It is the commercial peak of Paycheck's outlaw-adjacent phase, even though the title song's credit belongs to a fellow outlaw artist rather than Paycheck himself.
lineage: Its title song, written by David Allan Coe, is direct evidence of the outlaw scene's songwriter-sharing culture, and the album's success made Paycheck a mainstream outlaw figure alongside Jennings and Nelson.
key_tracks: Take This Job and Shove It

label: Epic Records
description: A tribute album of ten Merle Haggard songs, including two duets with Haggard himself, recorded as Paycheck's outlaw-era hitmaking was winding down. Critics have long treated it as one of the great late-night honky-tonk records, with Paycheck's rougher voice giving Haggard's songs a harder, more desperate edge than Haggard's own versions. It closes out the classic run of Paycheck albums that began with 11 Months and 29 Days and Take This Job and Shove It.
lineage: A direct homage to Bakersfield hard-country figure Merle Haggard, tying Paycheck's outlaw-era catalog back to the honky-tonk tradition the whole movement drew from.
key_tracks: I Can't Hold Myself in Line
borderline_note: Released in 1981, just after V23's usual 1971-1980 window, but it closes out Paycheck's outlaw-era Epic run and was explicitly named as a seed record for this lane.

album: Bobby Bare Sings Lullabys, Legends and Lies
label: RCA Victor
description: A double album written entirely by Shel Silverstein, mixing tall tales, ghost stories and barroom comedy over Bare's easygoing baritone. "Marie Laveau" became a number-one hit despite, or because of, its voodoo-queen storyline, and the record as a whole treats country songwriting as folklore and stand-up comedy at once. It is one of the clearest examples of outlaw-era Nashville making room for a writer as eccentric as Silverstein.
lineage: The start of Bare's long songwriting partnership with Shel Silverstein, which also produced Tompall Glaser's and Waylon Jennings's own Silverstein records.

label: RCA Victor
description: A more topical, less whimsical record than the Silverstein albums, opening with Ry Cooder's "The Cowboy and the Poet" and including Jerry Jeff Walker's "Up Against the Wall Redneck Mother," a barbed dig at rural Texas machismo. Bare's plainspoken baritone treats the songs as reportage as much as entertainment, closer to the socially observant end of outlaw-adjacent Nashville songwriting. It shows Bare's ear for outside songwriters beyond his usual Silverstein partnership.
lineage: Follows Lullabys, Legends and Lies in Bare's mid-1970s run of song-interpreter albums, this time drawing on the Texas progressive-country scene around Jerry Jeff Walker.
key_tracks: Up Against the Wall Redneck Mother
The Cowboy and the Poet (Faster Horses)

label: RCA Victor
description: A concept album by Shel Silverstein about poverty and hard luck in mid-1970s America, released the same year as Cowboys and Daddys, moving through unemployment lines, alimony payments and pocket change with dark comic detail. Bare's warm, conversational baritone keeps songs about economic desperation from turning into pure misery, closer to Prine-style funny-sad songwriting than protest music. It is one of the more overtly political records to come out of the outlaw-adjacent Nashville scene.
lineage: A second 1975 collaboration with Shel Silverstein after Lullabys, Legends and Lies, extending Bare's run of concept records built around outside songwriters.

label: MGM Records
description: Recorded with members of the Allman Brothers Band's circle and the Marshall Tucker Band's Toy Caldwell, this album marked Hank Williams Jr.'s break from his father's shadow toward a harder, Southern-rock-inflected sound. It arrived not long before Williams's near-fatal 1975 mountain-climbing fall, and its mix of outlaw defiance and rock-band guests set the direction his career would take after he recovered. It is generally treated as the record where he stopped being a Hank Williams tribute act.
lineage: Bridges outlaw country and Southern rock directly, pulling Allman Brothers and Marshall Tucker Band musicians into a Nashville country session.

label: Elektra/Curb
description: By 1979 Hank Williams Jr. had fully absorbed Southern rock and outlaw country into a single rowdy sound, and this album's title track and "Outlaw Women" made the fusion explicit. It is louder and more guitar-driven than the Nashville mainstream of the time, aimed at the same audience Waylon Jennings and the Allman Brothers shared. The record became one of his signature statements and a bridge toward the arena-country sound he committed to fully in the 1980s.
lineage: The clearest outlaw-country-to-Southern-rock crossover record of the decade, and a direct precursor to the harder-edged mainstream country Williams built through the 1980s.

album: Help Me Make It Through the Night
label: Mega Records
description: Sammi Smith's smoky, unhurried reading of the title track, a Kris Kristofferson song, became a crossover hit and won the CMA Award for Single of the Year, turning a little-known Mega Records singer into one of outlaw country's few prominent female voices. The rest of the album leans on the same behind-the-beat, late-night phrasing, closer to a smoky bar than a Nashville showcase. It is a key document of how Kristofferson's songwriting reached listeners years before his own albums did.
lineage: Built around a Kris Kristofferson song recorded before his own version reached wide audiences, tying Smith's career directly to the outlaw movement's key songwriter.
key_tracks: Help Me Make It Through the Night
borderline_note: Released in 1970, just before V23's usual 1971 start, but it is the definitive early recording of a Kristofferson song and a direct forerunner of the movement.

label: A&M Records
description: Steve Young's debut, recorded in Los Angeles with country-rock session players, introduced "Seven Bridges Road," the song that later became a hit for the Eagles. It predates the outlaw movement's commercial rise by several years but shares its songwriter-first, unpolished ethic, closer to a folk troubadour than a Nashville product. Young's rough, plainspoken baritone and the record's blend of Southern gospel and country-rock textures make it a direct forerunner of the Waylon Jennings and Billy Joe Shaver records that followed.
lineage: A direct influence on the outlaw sound that followed: its title track was covered by Waylon Jennings on Lonesome, On'ry and Mean, and Seven Bridges Road later became an Eagles hit.
borderline_note: Released in 1969, two years before V23's usual start date, but it directly seeded the outlaw sound: its title track was covered by Waylon Jennings and Seven Bridges Road became a standard.

label: Reprise Records
description: Young's second album re-recorded the title track from his debut and added his own "Lonesome, On'ry and Mean," the same year Waylon Jennings covered that song as an album title track, alongside originals about drifting and disillusionment. Produced by David Briggs, who also worked with Neil Young, it has a similarly loose, unhurried country-rock feel. It remains a cult favorite among outlaw-country collectors despite selling little on release.
lineage: Shares producer David Briggs with Neil Young's Crazy Horse records, and its songs Seven Bridges Road and Lonesome, On'ry and Mean both became touchstones for the outlaw movement.

label: RCA Records
description: Young covers Townes Van Zandt's title track and Bob Dylan's "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right" alongside a rerecording of his own "Seven Bridges Road," making explicit his place in the same songwriter's-songwriter lineage as Van Zandt and Guy Clark. It is a quieter, more acoustic-leaning record than the outlaw movement's rowdier entries, closer to Texas songwriter tradition than Nashville road-band sound. The record closes out Young's most productive decade without ever giving him the commercial recognition his songs earned other people.
lineage: Draws directly on Townes Van Zandt's songwriting, linking the outlaw scene's Nashville wing to the Texas singer-songwriter tradition centered on Van Zandt and Guy Clark.
key_tracks: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right

label: MCA Records
description: Lee Clayton's self-titled debut introduced "Ladies Love Outlaws," the song that gave the whole movement one of its defining phrases after Waylon Jennings turned it into an album title the following year. Clayton was reportedly unhappy with the record's standard Nashville production, but the songwriting itself set the rough-living, wandering persona that outlaw country would run with. It remains more important for its title track's afterlife than for its own commercial impact.
lineage: Its title track directly named Waylon Jennings's 1972 album Ladies Love Outlaws and helped coin the movement's own name.

label: Capitol Records
description: Clayton's Capitol debut is best known for "Silver Stallion," later recorded by the Highwaymen supergroup of Jennings, Nelson, Kristofferson and Cash, even though the album itself sold poorly on release. Its widescreen, guitar-driven songs about borders, drifting and lost love sit closer to Marty Robbins's gunfighter ballads than to barroom outlaw rock. Critics treated it warmly at the time, but commercial failure kept Clayton a cult figure rather than a star.
lineage: Its title track's companion song Silver Stallion was later covered by the Highwaymen, tying Clayton directly back to the movement's biggest names.
key_tracks: If You Can Touch Her At All

label: Capitol Records
description: Clayton's most commercially successful album, driven by the single "I Ride Alone," whose talky, Dylan-indebted delivery matches the record's restless, drifting persona. Songs like Saturday Night Special push the outlaw scene's drug-and-gun subject matter further than most of Clayton's peers were willing to go on record. It closed out the 1970s as Clayton's commercial high point before he largely disappeared from recording.
lineage: Clayton's commercial peak, extending the outlaw persona he introduced on his 1973 debut into more explicit, harder-edged territory.

artist: Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser
label: RCA Victor
description: RCA's marketing department assembled previously released tracks by Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser under a Wild West-themed cover, coining "outlaw" as a genre label almost by accident. It became the first country album certified platinum, proving there was a large audience for artists RCA's Nashville system had spent years trying to smooth out. Anchored by the Jennings-Nelson duet Good Hearted Woman and the Jennings-Colter duet Suspicious Minds, it turned a loose community of like-minded artists into a recognized movement with a name and a sales chart to prove it.
lineage: The compilation that named and commercially confirmed the outlaw country movement, gathering the four artists whose Hillbilly Central-adjacent records define this lane.
key_tracks: My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys
